newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices extend downturn as Iraq throws switch.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices extend downturn as Iraq throws switch.

text.p: Oil prices fell Tuesday after Iraq reopened a pipeline -- although neighbouring Turkey said no oil arrived -- to resume oil exports after a six-year halt and suggested it would ratchet up sales.
On other markets, coffee prices rebounded from last week's drop. Tight supplies of coffee for immediate delivery and good demand from coffee roasters lifted prices.

Energy markets also were put under pressure by a forecast calling for warmer weather in the Northeast that should lessen demand for energy in the world's largest heating oil market. The region was hit by heavy snow over the weekend.

In Iraq, President Saddam Hussein reopened the oil pipeline that will carry Iraqi oil through Turkey back to the world market for the first time since 1990, although the oil failed to flow immediately because of a malfunction.
Nevertheless, Iraq had moved swiftly on United Nations approval of its oil-for-food deal, submitting oil contracts.

The renewable deal allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil, or less than 600,000 barrels a day, over six months, with the proceeds used to buy humanitarian aid. Iraqi oil exports will make only a slight difference in the world market, where demand is 72 million barrels a day.
Still, Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said Iraq hoped to double the amount of oil it is allowed to ship to after three months.
"We have every hope that there should be an increase in oil exports ... either by 50 percent or double the amount," Rasheed said.
"There is a lot indication that if they (Iraq) can move oil, then they will. That created selling pressure in a continuation from yesterday," said Merrill Lynch analyst Michael Rothman.
Crude for January delivery fell 88 cents to $24.42 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
January heating oil dropped 2.51 cents to 69.62 cents a gallon, January gasoline sank 2.02 cents to 66.86 cents a gallon. January natural gas rebounded 17.4 cents to $3.396 per 1,000 cubic feet.
"A lot of this is weather related. The forecast was orginally for cold, and now it's going to be warmer," said Al Lindseth, a trader with GSC Energy.
The National Weather Service's six- to 10-day outlook called for above normal temperatures in the Northeast.
Coffee prices rose sharply in a technical correction to last week's slide to seven-week lows.
December coffee jumped 4.65 cents to 117.75 cents a pound at the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange.
Supplies for spot delivery were fairly tight, and there was a lot of uncertainty about the size of Brazil's next crop, the world's largest.

"The question is, how big is the 1997/98 Brazilian crop?" said Hencorp Becstone President Victor Henriquez. "If it is less than 1996/97 (which was put at 27 million 132-pound bags), with the drawdown in stock levels, tightness we see now is going to be a reality next year."
